subject: chemistry
title: The periodic table and its trends

scenes.heading: The periodic table and its trends
scenes.sub: Predict how an element behaves just from where it sits
scenes.say: The periodic table is the chemist's most useful tool. Once you know its patterns, you can predict how an element behaves just from where it sits.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Supermarket aisles keep similar things together
scenes.science: Groups (columns) share the same valence electrons
scenes.breaks: Supermarkets choose their layout; the table's pattern comes from atomic number and electron arrangement.
scenes.say: The periodic table is like a supermarket. Groups, the columns, are like aisles: elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons, so they behave alike. Periods, the rows, are like shelf levels: each row down adds another electron shell.

scenes.heading: How it's organised
points: Ordered by atomic NUMBER, not mass
Metals on the left, non-metals on the right
Mendeleev left gaps and predicted elements
scenes.say: Elements are ordered by atomic number, not mass. Metals sit on the left, non-metals on the right, and metalloids like silicon sit along the staircase line. Mendeleev left gaps for undiscovered elements, and his correct predictions supported the table.

scenes.heading: Two key groups
scenes.say: Alkali metals in group one lose their one outer electron and react with water. Lithium fizzes gently, sodium whizzes around, and potassium bursts into a lilac flame. Halogens in group seventeen gain one electron, so fluorine is the most reactive. Metals get keener going down; halogens get lazier.

scenes.heading: Why metals get keener
scenes.everyday: A dog on a long lead pulls free more easily
scenes.science: A far-away, shielded outer electron is lost more easily
scenes.breaks: A dog pulls itself away; an electron isn't trying to escape – it's removed when the atom reacts.
scenes.say: Going down group one, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, with more inner shells shielding it. It's like a dog on a long lead: much easier to pull free. So the electron is lost more easily, and the metal is more reactive.

scenes.heading: Atomic size
scenes.say: Atoms get bigger down a group, because each period adds a shell. Across a period they get smaller, because more protons pull the same shells in tighter, like a stronger magnet. So the biggest atoms are bottom-left, and the smallest are top-right.

scenes.heading: Halogen displacement
scenes.question: Will iodine react with potassium chloride solution?
lines: Iodine is below chlorine in group 17
scenes.say: For halogen displacement, the higher one wins. Iodine is below chlorine, so it's less reactive, and it can't push chlorine out. No reaction. But chlorine with potassium bromide does react, making orange-brown bromine.

Quick recap. Groups go down, periods go across. Alkali metals get more reactive down the group, halogens less. Atoms are biggest at the bottom-left. And the higher halogen wins. Now try the practice questions!
